interviewQuestions.question: How would you design the on-call rotation and paging for this system?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd treat this as a design decision tied to the system's architecture, not an operational afterthought: alerts route to the team that owns the failing component, with a clear, time-boxed escalation path — a primary rotation, escalating to a secondary after 15 minutes unacknowledged, then to a team lead.

I'd point to a concrete before/after: paging the checkout team directly for a checkout alert, instead of a generic 'backend on-call,' cut average time-to-first-response from 12 minutes down to under 2, because the generic on-call engineer was previously spending most of that time just figuring out who owned the problem.

I'd size the rotation itself deliberately too — at least 4-6 engineers, so no one person's on-call burden exceeds roughly a week a month, since a smaller rotation burns people out and eventually loses coverage entirely.

**Testing:** whether you treat paging and ownership mapping as an architectural decision, not an afterthought bolted on after launch.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Ownership-based routing as a design decision

interviewQuestions.question: An alert fires for a shared dependency that three teams depend on — who gets paged?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd page the team that actually owns the shared dependency — they're the only ones who can fix it — and notify, rather than page, the three teams that depend on it, so they have visibility into the incident without diluting responsibility for the actual fix.

I'd explain why paging all three consuming teams is worse than it sounds: it creates uncoordinated, duplicated response, similar to the multiple-engineers-colliding failure mode from incident response, without adding any real fixing capability, since none of the three teams owns the component that's actually broken. The fix is entirely on the owning team's side.

**Testing:** whether you can extend ownership-based routing correctly to a shared-dependency edge case, not just the simple single-owner path.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Follow-up: routing for a shared dependency

interviewQuestions.question: How do you know if your on-call load is sustainable, versus burning people out?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd track pages-per-shift and off-hours pages per person over time, rather than just confirming the rotation is technically staffed. A sustained rise in either metric — especially in low-value, non-actionable pages — is the leading indicator to act on before an engineer burns out or leaves the rotation, not something to notice only after the fact.

I'd feed this metric back into two levers: alert quality (are the pages actually actionable, or noise that should be tuned out) and rotation size (is the load actually spread across enough people). I'd frame sustainability as an ongoing measurement, not a one-time check, since both alert volume and team size drift over time as the system evolves.

**Testing:** whether you have a concrete, measurable signal for burnout risk, not just a hope that people will speak up before quitting.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Follow-up: measuring on-call sustainability
